_note: ALL NUMBERS ARE PLACEHOLDERS for gameplay.

mass.title: Puzzle 1: Mass
mass.intro: Pack a photo satellite into a 3.6 kg rocket slot.
mass.lesson: Mass, power and data are linked: a faster radio needs more power, and power needs mass.

needs.missing: You need a camera to take photos.
You need solar panels for power.
You need a battery for the dark part of the orbit.
You need a radio to send the photos down.

why_hard: Four limits at once: mass, money, power and data rate.
The camera makes 60 MB of photos a week. 40 MB must reach the ground.
Every radio and antenna uses power, and power comes from heavy panels.
Fixing one limit often breaks another.
goal: A camera, panels, a battery and a radio
Panels make at least the power used
Send at least 40 MB a week

power.title: Puzzle 2: Power
power.intro: Keep the satellite alive through the dark part of every orbit.
power.lesson: Panels must make enough power on average, and the battery must cover the eclipse.
why_hard: It needs 12 W every minute, day and night.
The Earth blocks the Sun for 35 of every 95 minutes.
In sunlight the panels must run the satellite AND refill the battery.
A bigger battery is heavier. Limit: 0.7 kg.
goal: Full again before the next eclipse

link.title: Puzzle 3: Data link
link.intro: The camera makes 60 MB of photos a week, but the radio sends only 36 MB. Find a way to get 40 MB a week to the ground.
link.lesson: The slowest step sets the pace. The best fixes are often free: change how you use what you already have.

options.label: Bolt on a big antenna
options.why: It works, but 0.4 kg is more than the 0.3 kg you have left.

options.label: Rent a second ground station
options.why: More passes over a station means more time to send. Costly, but simple.

options.label: Take smaller photos
options.why: Less data to send, but the radio still only manages 36 MB a week.

options.label: Only photograph coastlines
options.why: Smart: skip photos you do not need. But sending is still the bottleneck.

options.label: Compress photos on board
options.detail: Radio carries +10 MB/wk of photos, $20k, 2 W
options.why: Software, not hardware: the same radio carries more photos. Costs computer power.

options.label: Run the radio at full power
options.why: Free speed, but it needs 4 W and you only have 3 W spare. Can you free some power?

options.label: Switch off the camera heater in sunlight
options.why: The camera is warm enough in the Sun. This frees power for something else.

options.label: Save photos and send them later
options.why: A trap: storage only delays the problem. The radio still sends 36 MB a week.

options.label: Rent a relay satellite
options.why: Very fast, and far too expensive for this mission.

why_hard: Data only counts once it reaches the ground.
The slowest step in the chain sets the pace.
You have 0.3 kg, $120k and 3 W of power to spare. No more.
Not every idea helps. Some only look like they do.

time.title: Puzzle 4: Budget and time
time.intro: Plan the year so the satellite is ready for its rocket without running out of money. Then play the year: real projects always hit surprises.
time.lesson: Start the paperwork early, leave room for surprises, and never skip testing: a fault found on the ground costs days, a fault found in orbit costs the mission.

surprises.text: Testing found a loose cable on the radio. Fixing it took 10 extra days.
surprises.missed: Short testing missed a loose cable. In orbit the launch shaking had worked it free and the radio went silent. Real missions such as Vanguard TV-3 and Hitomi were lost to faults that got through.

surprises.text: The licence office asked for more details about your camera. The licence took 15 days longer.

why_hard: Build, then test, then ship: each waits for the one before.
The licence runs alongside, but takes 120 days.
The team is paid every day until shipping.
Rushing is faster, but costs more.
